title: Very short, reliable curative treatment for active and latent tuberculosis

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a safe, reliable tuberculosis treatment delivered in a single dose or a comparably short, practical regimen. Its intended scope includes both treating people with latent TB infection to prevent future disease and curing people who already have active TB, including relevant drug-resistant forms. These are separate clinical indications: success in one would not establish success in the others, and different regimens could be needed.

Conceptual distinction: preventing progression from latent infection to active disease is different from demonstrating that latent infection has been cleared. The former is the preventive endpoint proposed here; the latter is a stronger interpretation of the curative ambition in the title and would require additional evidence. Likewise, a short administration schedule and a short period of drug exposure are different properties: a long-acting injection could simplify dosing while continuing to release medicine over time.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: if a single dose or comparably simple regimen proved safe and effective, it would greatly simplify treatment completion relative to prolonged treatment. For active disease, the central benefit would be achieving durable cure with far less treatment burden. For latent infection, it would be delivering effective prevention through a much simpler intervention. These benefits do not depend on claiming that preventive treatment has demonstrated complete bacterial clearance.

Conditional downstream possibilities include broader treatment uptake, more completed courses and improved population-level TB control. Their scale would depend on diagnosis, access, delivery and the regimen’s actual effectiveness across the populations treated. Even an exceptional treatment would not by itself establish a route to eradication: prevention, surveillance and the ability to identify and reach people needing treatment would remain consequential.

The ambition combines infectious-disease therapeutics with drug delivery and pharmacology. A convenient formulation would be revolutionary only if it also produced the required clinical outcomes. Neither a one-dose administration schedule nor a favorable laboratory endpoint alone would establish reliable human cure, prevention across populations or effectiveness against resistant disease.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed scientific requirement: the regimen must produce durable benefit despite the biological differences between latent infection and active disease. The supplied research identifies persistent bacteria, differing tissue environments and differing bacterial burdens as central challenges. These are retained as the concept’s stated scientific rationale, but the supplied review had no usable scientific source text with which to substantiate those biological assertions.

Proposed engineering requirement: a very short administration schedule must deliver sufficient treatment where it is needed, with acceptable safety, while avoiding relapse and the emergence or selection of resistance. A long-acting formulation would need an appropriate exposure profile as well as convenient administration. The supplied evidence does not establish that sorfequiline, or any other regimen, meets these requirements for the full intended scope.

The clinical breakthrough would require separate evidence for preventive treatment, drug-susceptible active TB and the drug-resistant forms included in the eventual claim. Demonstrating latent-infection clearance would introduce a further measurement problem: the evidence would have to support clearance itself, rather than infer it solely from fewer cases of subsequent disease. The supplied materials do not resolve how that stronger endpoint would be established.

current_state.text: The supplied citation metadata identifies a purported study by Li and colleagues titled “One-Dose Efficacy of Long-Acting Sorfequiline in a Mouse Model of Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy,” described in the research as a bioRxiv preprint dated September 22, 2026, with DOI 10.64898/2026.09.22.752266. The earlier research says that the study tested long-acting injectable sorfequiline and reported that 92% of mice receiving at least 125 mg/kg were culture-negative at 12 weeks. Those details are preserved as reported claims, not verified experimental findings: the supplied review could not inspect the study identity, publication status, experimental methods or results.

The access limitation is material. Although the earlier candidate said that a preprint abstract had been assessed, the retained HTML examined in the supplied review contained only a cookie-access notice and no scientific abstract. The source index records retrieval on November 11, 2026, and marks the artifact as saved, verified and untruncated, but those capture attributes do not verify the paper’s identity or scientific claims. An untruncated access notice is still an incomplete basis for evaluating a study.

Conditional interpretation of the reported experiment: even if the mouse result is confirmed, a preventive-therapy model would provide preclinical evidence within that model. A culture-negative result at the reported 12-week endpoint would not by itself establish human latent-infection eradication, durable human preventive efficacy or a single-dose cure for active TB. It would also leave drug-resistant active disease and the broader clinical safety claim to be demonstrated separately.

Evidence boundary: the supplied search record is empty, so these materials do not establish comprehensive research coverage, subsequent developments or whether the innovation had been achieved or remained open as of November 1, 2026. They also do not substantiate a human demonstration of the full concept. The inaccessible scientific text is a verification gap, not evidence that the reported study or its findings are false; there is no supplied basis for calling the result scientifically disputed.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: independently replicated clinical trials would show that a single dose or a comparably short, practical regimen safely prevents progression to active TB in people with latent infection and separately produces durable cure in people with active TB. If separate regimens are required, each should have its own indication-specific evidence. Animal preventive efficacy would be an intermediate contribution, not completion of these human clinical goals.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated trials establish safe short-regimen TB prevention and durable cure

completion_criteria.text: For active disease, the proposed evidence package should cover drug-susceptible TB and explicitly defined, clinically relevant drug-resistant forms, with follow-up sufficient to assess relapse after treatment. For preventive treatment, it should assess subsequent disease over a prespecified follow-up period. Any claim of clearing latent infection should be evaluated separately through evidence capable of supporting that stronger conclusion.
completion_criteria.label: Evidence covers drug-susceptible and defined drug-resistant TB with indication-specific follow-up

completion_criteria.text: An operational protocol would need to define acceptable efficacy and safety, the maximum administration schedule qualifying as very short, the resistant-disease coverage claimed, and the duration and completeness of follow-up. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards supplied by the evidence. The historical greater-than-95% efficacy figure is not adopted as a validated threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Protocol defines efficacy, safety and operational treatment qualification criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence would include independent confirmation, sufficiently transparent methods and results, and evaluation under conditions relevant to delivery. For a long-acting injection, assessment should distinguish the number of administrations from the duration of drug exposure. Claims should remain bounded by the populations, disease forms and delivery conditions actually studied; finite trials establish demonstrated breadth, not universal effectiveness.
completion_criteria.label: Transparent, independently confirmed evidence establishes practical limits of treatment claims

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: INF-03, “A tuberculosis vaccine that interrupts transmission,” is the closest disease-specific complement. INF-03 seeks to interrupt transmission through vaccination; INF-12 seeks much simpler preventive treatment and cure after infection. Their public-health effects could reinforce one another, but evidence for a treatment would not demonstrate vaccine-mediated interruption of transmission.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-05, “Near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections,” could help identify who needs treatment and inform treatment selection. That diagnostic capability remains distinct from delivering durable TB cure. INF-06, “A dependable platform for generating new antibacterial treatments,” overlaps with the discovery of effective TB drugs, whereas INF-12 requires a specific clinical outcome and administration schedule. INF-15, “A rapidly adaptable clinical phage-therapy platform,” is another therapeutic-platform concept; nothing supplied establishes it as a solution to this TB treatment goal.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-02, “A safe, scalable cure for established HIV infection,” and INF-11, “A safe, broadly effective treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B,” share the ambition of durable benefit after treatment ends. Their pathogen biology and cure endpoints remain distinct from TB. INF-07, “Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections,” instead emphasizes breadth across pathogens, while INF-12 emphasizes treatment simplicity and durable outcomes across specified states of one infection.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-01, the broadly protective HIV vaccine; INF-08, the pre-emptive pandemic-coronavirus vaccine; INF-09, the rapid end-to-end vaccine response; and INF-13, the durable, readily deliverable malaria vaccine, all concern vaccination rather than the therapeutic capability proposed here. INF-04 targets malaria transmission through vectors. INF-10 seeks prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus, and INF-14 seeks mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes. These entries share broader prevention or disease-control ambitions with INF-12, but none supplies evidence that very short TB treatment has been achieved.

unresolved_issues: The identity, authorship, September 22, 2026 date, DOI and preprint status of the purported sorfequiline study remain unverified from the retained scientific source content.
The mouse model, dose threshold, 92% culture-negative finding and 12-week endpoint require usable study text; their absence from the retained artifact does not show that they are false.
The supplied materials do not substantiate the biological rationale concerning tissue environments, bacterial persistence, bacterial burden, relapse or resistance.
The empty search record leaves research coverage and subsequent developments unknown; no comprehensive current-state conclusion can be drawn for November 1, 2026 or the later retrieval date.

The final scope must specify whether preventing progression is sufficient for the latent-infection indication or whether demonstrable clearance is required. No method for establishing the stronger clearance claim is supplied.

Acceptable efficacy, safety, administration duration, resistant-disease coverage and follow-up remain to be defined. The greater-than-95% figure is not an established standard in the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Tuberculosis treatment finished in very few doses
possible: People with tuberculosis (TB) could receive a lasting cure through a single dose or a similarly short, practical course, including for forms that resist existing medicines.
People with latent TB, an infection that has not caused active disease, could receive equally simple treatment to prevent future illness. Prevention and cure could require different medicines.
why: Much simpler treatment would reduce the burden on patients and make courses easier to finish. More people could take up treatment and complete it, helping communities control TB.

sources.showed: In mice, injections sustained drug levels linked to killing bacteria. The preprint, awaiting journal review, tested sorfequiline, a TB drug delivered through long-acting injectable (LAI) formulations that release medicine over time.
sources.quote: All tested LAI formulations achieved this target for at least 4 weeks post-dose.
sources.cited_for: The study supports testing an injection that releases medicine over time for TB prevention.
sources.not_established: A mouse prevention experiment does not establish safe prevention or lasting cure in people.

sources.showed: A month of rifapentine plus isoniazid, medicines used against TB, prevented disease at least as well as a longer course of isoniazid in people with HIV.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports shortening preventive treatment in people.
sources.not_established: It did not establish prevention through a single dose, clearance of latent infection or cure of active disease.

sources.showed: A four-month treatment containing rifapentine and moxifloxacin, medicines used against TB, worked at least as well as the control treatment for active disease.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports shortening treatment for active TB.
sources.not_established: It did not establish a very short cure or effectiveness across the intended drug-resistant forms.

sources.who: Bern-Thomas Nyang’wa and the TB-PRACTECAL Study Collaborators
sources.showed: A course of pills treated lung TB resistant to rifampin, an antibiotic, at least as well as standard care, with better safety. Recruitment ended early.
sources.quote:
In patients with rifampin-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, a 24-week, all-oral 
regimen was noninferior to the accepted standard-care treatment, and it had a 
better safety profile.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports shorter oral treatment for a defined form of drug-resistant TB.
sources.not_established: Treatment still lasted months and did not establish a very short cure across drug-resistant forms.

shown: Human trials have shortened both prevention and treatment, but courses still take weeks or months. Swindells and colleagues demonstrated effective month-long prevention in people with HIV.

Li and colleagues moved closer to the dosing ambition in mice: 92% receiving higher doses had no bacteria grow from tested samples. This early, unreviewed result concerns a prevention model, not human cure.
missing: Human trials have yet to establish safe prevention and lasting active-disease cure with a single dose or comparably short course.
Separate evidence must establish effectiveness against the drug-resistant forms claimed and track disease returning after treatment.
Very short dosing must deliver enough medicine safely without encouraging resistance.
Any claim that latent infection has been cleared needs evidence beyond fewer subsequent cases of disease.

milestones.label: Independent trials establish safe prevention and lasting cure
milestones.explanation: Independently repeated human trials would have to establish safe prevention and lasting cure with very short treatment. Separate results would establish each use, including any different medicines needed.

milestones.label: Results cover the claimed disease forms and later outcomes
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to cover TB responsive to existing drugs and defined resistant forms, tracking later disease or return after cure. Any claim of clearing latent infection would need separate proof.

milestones.label: Clear rules define what counts as successful treatment
milestones.explanation: A protocol would have to define acceptable benefit, safety, dosing duration, resistant forms covered and follow-up. These rules would make success judgeable.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation establishes practical limits
milestones.explanation: Transparent studies and independent confirmation would have to establish results under relevant delivery conditions, distinguishing dosing from drug-release duration. This would define whom treatment can reliably help.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether preventing active disease is sufficient for latent TB or whether complete bacterial clearance must also be demonstrated.
Acceptable safety, effectiveness, dosing duration and follow-up still need clear thresholds.
An injection may finish dosing quickly while releasing medicine much longer; how that should qualify as very short treatment remains open.

page.title: Single-dose tuberculosis treatment and prevention
page.definition: Regimens given once prevent tuberculosis (TB) disease in people with infection but no disease, and separately produce relapse-free cure of drug-susceptible and rifampicin-resistant lung TB; rifampicin is a first-line antibiotic. Long-acting formulations release medicine after dosing, and preventive efficacy measures subsequent disease rather than clearance of infection.

goal.need: WHO estimates that 10.6 million people developed TB and 1.13 million died from it in 2025. In the randomized BRIEF TB/A5279 prevention trial, a shorter regimen increased treatment completion while meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion.

figures.caption: Treatment completion in BRIEF TB/A5279, published in 2019
figures.note: The trial enrolled 3000 people with HIV. Completion percentages measure completion of medication, not protection against TB.

statements.quote: The profile for TB preventive treatment aims at a full course given as a single injection at one encounter.
our goal of developing an ultra-short regimen capable of treating both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant TB.
statements.context: President and CEO Mel Spigelman discussing NC-009 results on 19 November 2025. This passage does not define a duration or dose count.

completion.title: FDA approves single-dose regimens for TB prevention and susceptible and rifampicin-resistant lung TB.
completion.criterion: FDA grants traditional approval, based on clinical benefit, for complete drug regimens given at one dosing encounter with no oral lead-in or later TB doses, separately for TB prevention in people with infection but no disease, drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, and rifampicin-resistant pulmonary TB. Different regimens and defined labelled populations are allowed. Active-disease evidence establishes survival, culture negativity and absence of relapse or recurrence over protocol-defined follow-up; preventive evidence establishes reduced progression to disease. Drug-release duration is recorded separately from dosing.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; FDA supplies the approval standard but has not set this combined single-dose target.
completion.basis: Searched WHO’s 2020 preventive-treatment product profile, 2023 active-TB regimen profiles and 2026 injectable profiles, FDA’s May 2026 TB guidance, and single-dose trial registrations. No joint single-dose completion criterion was found. WHO’s injectable targets allow up to 4 months and 3 dosing encounters for active disease. The Atlas therefore combines a one-encounter dosing boundary with FDA’s existing approval test, without adding an efficacy percentage or a universal follow-up interval.

milestones.title: A TB candidate reduces bacterial burden or sterilizes infection in a validated model.
milestones.criterion: The candidate reduces bacterial burden or produces sterilizing activity in a validated TB infection model, with exposure–response data supporting dose selection. The abstract of the 22 September 2026 sorfequiline preprint reports 92% culture negativity at 12 weeks after a single injection of at least 125 mg/kg in a preventive-therapy mouse model; the denominator is not given. This result is not peer reviewed and does not establish relapse-free cure.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, May 2026 guidance, section III.C.1(a). This guidance concerns pulmonary TB drug development; it specifies model endpoints without a numerical efficacy cutoff.

milestones.title: A TB candidate’s IND takes effect after 30 days without a hold, or FDA permits an earlier start.
milestones.criterion: For the US pathway, an IND (investigational new drug application) takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless the investigation is placed on clinical hold, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigation may begin. The milestone is an effective IND for the proposed TB regimen and dosing schedule.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.40(b).
milestones.threshold_quote: On earlier notification by FDA that the clinical investigations in the IND may begin.

milestones.title: A TB candidate is administered to people in a phase 1 pharmacology and safety study.
milestones.criterion: Initial human administration occurs in a closely monitored phase 1 study designed to characterize drug exposure and adverse effects. RespiriTB’s project report, updated on 22 December 2025, records the start of a first-in-human study of intramuscular long-acting bedaquiline, enrolling 32 healthy volunteers across three dose groups. This project report is not peer reviewed; it establishes entry into human testing, without establishing preventive efficacy.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, definition of phase 1 in 21 CFR 312.21(a).
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A TB regimen provides preliminary human efficacy evidence supporting phase 3 evaluation.
milestones.criterion: Controlled phase 2 studies provide indication-specific preliminary effectiveness and short-term risk data. The NC-009 oral-regimen protocol specifies stable sputum culture conversion over 8 weeks in at least 300 planned adults with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. On 19 November 2025, TB Alliance reported greater activity with daily 100 mg sorfequiline plus pretomanid and linezolid than with standard isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. These interim results were not peer reviewed. The regimen included further oral treatment and did not test single-dose therapy.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, entry condition for phase 3 in 21 CFR 312.21(c). NC-009’s example endpoint was set by TB Alliance for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB.
milestones.threshold_quote: preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

milestones.title: A single-dose TB regimen establishes clinical benefit in an adequate, controlled human investigation.
milestones.criterion: An adequate, controlled human investigation establishes clinical benefit of the single-dose regimen, with supporting safety data. Longer-course precedents met their prespecified noninferiority margins: BRIEF TB (2019; n=3000 with HIV; median follow-up 3.3 years), 1-month prevention, 1.25 events/100 person-years; Study 31 (2021; n=2516 randomized), 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin, 6.6 percentage points at 12 months; TB-PRACTECAL (2022; n=145 in the interim intention-to-treat analysis), 24-week bedaquiline–pretomanid–linezolid–moxifloxacin, 12 points at 72 weeks; recruitment stopped early. These are longer-course benchmarks.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.126 and May 2026 pulmonary TB guidance. The quoted treatment-effect criterion concerns pulmonary disease; BRIEF TB supplies a preventive-treatment protocol precedent. Each trial’s numerical margin belongs to that protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: a clinically meaningful and statistically robust treatment effect.

not_found: WHO’s full 2023 treatment-profile PDF and final 2026 injectable-profile PDF could not be retrieved; their official publication pages were accessible.
The sorfequiline mouse preprint’s full text could not be opened; its accessible PubMed abstract omits the mouse denominator.
No public FDA IND-effective notice for a complete single-dose TB regimen was located.
NC-009’s developer announcement does not state the analyzed sample size.
No completed human clinical efficacy result for a complete single-dose TB drug regimen was found in the registry and developer-pipeline searches.

results.finding: Single-dose sorfequiline LAI at ≥125 mg/kg rendered 23/25 (92%) mice culture-negative at 12 weeks in a validated paucibacillary TPT mouse model.
results.detail: Preprint; not peer reviewed. Culture negativity at 12 weeks in a preventive-therapy mouse model; exposure target Cmin 35 ng/mL and dose-ranging support dose selection. Does not establish relapse-free cure.
results.quote: In all, 23 of 25 (92%) mice receiving at least 125 mg/kg of any sorfequiline LAI formulation were rendered culture-negative at 12 weeks.

results.finding: 1-month daily rifapentine+isoniazid prevention in 3000 HIV-infected patients: TB/death incidence 0.65 vs 0.67 per 100 person-years.
results.detail: Randomized, open-label phase 3 noninferiority trial; 32/1488 vs 33/1498 events, rate difference −0.02/100 person-years, upper 95% CI 0.30; prevention in HIV-infected adults/adolescents. Regimen was daily for 1 month, not single-dose, so partial for m5.
results.quote: The primary end point was reported in 32 of 1488 patients (2%) in the 1-month group and in 33 of 1498 (2%) in the 9-month group, for an incidence rate of 0.65 per 100 person-years and 0.67 per 100 person-years, respectively

results.finding: Study 31: 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin vs standard 6-month regimen in 2516 randomized drug-susceptible TB patients; 15.5% vs 14.6% unfavorable outcome at 12 months.
results.detail: Phase 3, open-label, noninferiority trial of a 4-month oral regimen (rifapentine 1200 mg with or without moxifloxacin) versus 6-month standard therapy; noninferiority margin 6.6 percentage points, difference 1.0 point. No single-dose regimen was tested, so this is only a longer-course benchmark, not clinical benefit of a single-dose regimen.
results.quote: Rifapentine with moxifloxacin was noninferior to the control in the microbiologically eligible population (15.5% vs. 14.6% had an unfavorable outcome; difference, 1.0 percentage point; 95% confidence interval [CI], −2.6 to 4.5)

results.finding: Stage 1: 240 patients; BPaLM 77% culture conversion at 8 weeks; 8% discontinued or died.
results.detail: Controlled phase 2b stage within a phase 2–3 trial; 8-week culture conversion and short-term safety supported progression to stage 2. Regimen was 24-week, not single-dose.

results.finding: 128 modified ITT patients; 24-week BPaLM risk difference −37 percentage points at 72 weeks vs standard care.
results.detail: Longer-course benchmark; single-dose regimen not tested; recruitment terminated early. Supports clinical benefit for 24-week BPaLM, not the single-dose criterion.
results.quote: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, 11% of the patients in the BPaLM group and 48% of those in the standard-care group had a primary-outcome event (risk difference, −37 percentage points; 96.6% confidence interval [CI], −53 to −22).
